candidates.label: Seleucia Pieria archaeological site
candidates.support: Seleucia Pieria, the seaport of Antioch, about 16 miles from the city and about 5 miles north of the mouth of the Orontes. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on this coastal site; Wikidata's own record places it within Hatay Province, Türkiye.

scripture.textWEB: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus.

candidates.label: Attalia (modern Antalya)
candidates.support: A city on Pamphylia's coast founded by Attalus II Philadelphus, continuously inhabited today as Antalya, Türkiye. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site.

scripture.textWEB: When they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.

candidates.label: Samothrace (island)
candidates.support: An island in the north Aegean Sea, south of Thrace, with a town at its northern end where ships could anchor for the night. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the island, known today as Samothraki.

scripture.textWEB: Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;

candidates.label: Amphipolis archaeological site
candidates.support: A town in Macedonia on the river Strymon, on the Via Egnatia. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, which Wikidata places in today's municipality of Amphipolis.

scripture.textWEB: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.

candidates.label: Apollonia (Macedonia, on the Via Egnatia)
candidates.support: A town in Mygdonia, Macedonia, on the Via Egnatia between Amphipolis and Thessalonica, about 30 Roman miles from Amphipolis and 38 from Thessalonica. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, near the modern village of Nea Apollonia; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports that its name seems to survive in the modern Pollina.

scripture.textWEB: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.

candidates.label: Assos archaeological site
candidates.support: An ancient city of the Troad on a rocky height on the south coast, in the Roman province of Asia. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, known today as Behramkale, an alternate name recorded on the Wikidata item itself.

scripture.textWEB: But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had so arranged, intending himself to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.

candidates.label: Mitylene (chief city of Lesbos)
candidates.support: The chief city of the island of Lesbos, with two harbors. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, the modern city of Mytilene, Greece.

scripture.textWEB: When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.

candidates.label: Chios (island)
candidates.support: An Aegean island south of Lesbos, close to the Asia Minor mainland. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the island, which keeps the name Chios today. The point is the island's principal town, also called Chios.

scripture.textWEB: Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus.

candidates.label: Samos (island)
candidates.support: An Aegean island between Ephesus and Miletus, joined to the Roman province of Asia. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the island, which keeps the name Samos today.

scripture.textWEB: Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus.

candidates.label: Trogyllium (promontory opposite Samos)
candidates.support: A promontory on the Asia Minor coast opposite Samos, extending from the Mycale mountains, with an anchorage. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, which Pleiades identifies as today's Dip Burun. Several early manuscripts omit the clause naming it in Acts 20:15; see the route's note.

scripture.textWEB: Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus.

candidates.label: Cos (island)
candidates.support: An Aegean island off the coast of Caria, one of the six cities of the Dorian Hexapolis. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the island, known today as Kos.

scripture.textWEB: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

candidates.label: Rhodes (city)
candidates.support: The chief city of the island of Rhodes, in the southeastern Aegean. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the city of Rhodes as the site.

scripture.textWEB: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

candidates.label: Patara archaeological site
candidates.support: A coastal city of Lycia with a celebrated oracle of Apollo and a harbor serving trade with the interior. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives Gelemiş as the modern name of the ruin; Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site.

scripture.textWEB: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

candidates.label: Myra archaeological site
candidates.support: A Lycian city with a harbor used by grain ships from Alexandria. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site; Wikidata's own record places it within Demre district, Türkiye.

scripture.textWEB: When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.

candidates.label: Cnidus (Cape Krio / Tekir site)
candidates.support: A city of Caria at the end of a long, narrow peninsula, with two harbors. Pleiades records that in the late fourth century BC the city's political center moved here, to Tekir, from an older site at Burgaz, so the city Paul's ship passed was at Tekir. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the Tekir site; Wikidata's own record places it within Datça, Muğla Province, Türkiye.

scripture.textWEB: When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.

candidates.label: Salmone (promontory, Crete)
candidates.support: The promontory forming the northeastern corner of Crete. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, identified with today's Cape Sideros.

scripture.textWEB: When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.

candidates.label: Fair Havens (Kaloi Limenes)
candidates.support: A roadstead on Crete's south coast about 5 miles east of Cape Matala, sheltered from north and northwest winds but judged unsuitable for wintering. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site; its Greek name, Kaloi Limenes, is a direct translation of 'Fair Havens.'

scripture.textWEB: With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

candidates.label: Cauda (island south of Crete)
candidates.support: A small island south of Crete. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, identified with today's Gavdos, whose modern Greek name reflects the 'Cauda' manuscript reading rather than 'Clauda.'

scripture.textWEB: Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.

candidates.label: Sidon (ancient Phoenician port)
candidates.support: An ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, named in the Gospels alongside Tyre as well as in Acts. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, continuously inhabited today as Sidon, Lebanon.

scripture.textWEB: The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.
From there he arose and went away into the borders of Tyre and Sidon. He entered into a house and didn’t want anyone to know it, but he couldn’t escape notice.
Again he departed from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and came to the sea of Galilee through the middle of the region of Decapolis.

candidates.label: Syracuse (Sicily)
candidates.support: A Greek colony on Sicily's east coast and capital of the Roman province of Sicily. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, known today as Syracuse (Siracusa).

scripture.textWEB: Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.

candidates.label: Rhegium (Sicilian Strait)
candidates.support: A city on the Italian shore of the Sicilian Strait. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, known today as Reggio Calabria.

scripture.textWEB: From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,

candidates.label: Three Taverns (Tres Tabernae, Appian Way)
candidates.support: A station on the Appian Way about 33 Roman miles from Rome. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site.

scripture.textWEB: From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.

stops.name: Forum of Appius
stops.todayName: In the comune of Latina, Italy

candidates.label: Forum of Appius (Forum Appii, Appian Way)
candidates.support: A station on the Appian Way about 43 Roman miles from Rome, where a canal through the Pontine Marshes began. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site; Wikidata's own record places it within the comune of Latina, Italy. None of six popular English versions compared uses the World English Bible's wording, 'The Market of Appius'; three read 'Forum of Appius'. See the route's note.

scripture.textWEB: From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.

candidates.label: Ptolemais (Phoenician coast)
candidates.support: A Phoenician coastal city, identified with the Old Testament's Acco. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, known today as Acre (Akko).

scripture.textWEB: When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day.

candidates.label: Taybeh (et-Taiyibeh)
candidates.support: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the town Jesus retired to after raising Lazarus to be probably Eusebius's Ephrem, 5 Roman miles east of Bethel, and probably the village of et-Taiyibeh. Pleiades places Ephraim here, and OpenBible.info's leading identification and Wikidata's point for the modern village agree with Pleiades' coordinate to within about 0.1 km.

scripture.textWEB: Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews, but departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim. He stayed there with his disciples.

candidates.label: Et-Tur (Kafr et-Tur)
candidates.support: All six English versions compared spell the name 'Bethphage'; the WEB itself reads 'Bethsphage' at this and the other two passages below, the Majority Text's reading (footnoted in the NKJV). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia judges the summit of the Mount of Olives, where the village of Kefr et-Tur stands, the most probable site of New Testament Bethphage, 'much more probable' than Abu Dis, since the village 'certainly occupies an ancient site and no other name is known'; it places the medieval Bethphage between the summit and Bethany, at the site the Roman Catholics had enclosed. This point marks the Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land's sanctuary of Bethphage, on the eastern part of the Mount of Olives, where Wikidata and OpenBible.info also put Bethphage; OpenBible.info scores Et-Tur far above Abu Dis.

candidates.label: Abu Dis
candidates.support: A minority identification that the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia judges much less probable than Et-Tur; OpenBible.info scores it far below Et-Tur for the same identification. OpenBible.info and Wikidata give the same point for the village.

scripture.textWEB: When they came near to Jerusalem and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples,
When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,

candidates.label: Kursi (Gergesa)
candidates.support: The only one of the three candidates on the lake shore. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the event on the eastern shore, where 'the steep edges of the Bashan plateau drop close upon the brink of the lake', which it finds only just south of Wadi Semak, and takes the Gospels' Gerasa to be probably the ruins of Kurseh there; its 'Gadara' article likewise has Gadara's territory cover the country east of the lake, 'including the lands of the subordinate town, Gerasa'. OpenBible.info identifies Gergesa, the WEB's reading at Matthew 8:28, with Kursi.

candidates.label: Gadara
candidates.support: A Decapolis city (modern Umm Qais), about 6 miles southeast of the lake by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's estimate; the ship on its coins is, for that encyclopedia, proof that its territory reached the lake, so the area could be called the 'land of the Gadarenes', the WEB's reading at Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26, even though the city is not on the shore. OpenBible.info identifies Gadara, named at Matthew 8:28 in most English versions, with Umm Qais.

candidates.label: Gerasa (modern Jerash)
candidates.support: The best-known city of this name, far inland, about 19 miles from the Jordan by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's estimate. That encyclopedia takes the Gospels' Gerasa to be the Kursi site instead, but OpenBible.info identifies the Gerasa named at Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26 in most English versions with Jerash.

scripture.textWEB: When he came to the other side, into the country of the Gergesenes, two people possessed by demons met him there, coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that nobody could pass that way.
They came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes.
Then they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is opposite Galilee.

candidates.label: Loutro
candidates.support: A harbor on Crete's south coast, by the village of Loutro, sheltered from every wind. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls this the only safe harbor on this coast large enough for the ship, and states that the ancient authorities agree in placing Phoenix in this neighborhood, judging the identification "seems certain"; an inscription found at Loutro shows that Egyptian grain ships wintered there. It calls the harbor's east-facing aspect, against Acts 27:12's "looking southwest and northwest," a serious difficulty, and resolves it either by reading the phrase in sailors' language as looking down those winds, toward the northeast and southeast, which fits Loutro, or by supposing that the writer, who never saw Phoenix, described it wrongly. OpenBible.info rates this site its second identification (35% confidence). Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site.

candidates.label: Finikas
candidates.support: An open roadstead on the west side of the isthmus Loutro stands on. This reading takes Acts 27:12's "looking southwest and northwest" at face value; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records the proposal but judges the roadstead "not a suitable place for wintering in." OpenBible.info rates this site, at today's village of Finikas, its likelier identification (55% confidence, against 35% for Loutro), and Wikidata places the village here; Pleiades catalogs it as Phoinikous Limen.

scripture.textWEB: Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest.

candidates.label: Lasea ruins
candidates.support: A town on Crete's south coast about 5 miles east of Fair Havens and south of Gortyna, a city the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes had many Jews; its ruins were examined in 1856. The encyclopedia reasons that having to buy stores from Lasea, had the ship stayed at Fair Havens, helps explain the ship's reluctance to winter there instead of continuing toward Phoenix. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site.

scripture.textWEB: With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

candidates.label: Adramyttium (Karataş peninsula, Ören)
candidates.support: A city of Mysia, in the Roman province of Asia, with a good harbor at the head of the Gulf of Adramyttium, facing the island of Lesbos. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the city grew important once Pergamum became the province's capital, serving as the district's own administrative center, and that its ancient harbor has disappeared, while a village carrying a form of its name stands further inland. Pleiades places the ancient site on the modern Karataş peninsula at Ören; Wikidata and OpenBible.info agree, and Wikidata's own record places it within Balıkesir Province, Türkiye.

scripture.textWEB: Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica being with us.

candidates.label: Alexandria
candidates.support: A port city on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC by the isle of Pharos, and a major shipbuilding and trade center under Roman rule. Acts names "a ship of Alexandria" twice as the vessel Paul's party boarded: first at Myra (Acts 27:6), and again, after the shipwreck, on Malta (Acts 28:11); the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia confirms these as the New Testament's only two direct references to such a ship. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, continuously inhabited today as Alexandria, Egypt.

scripture.textWEB: There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose figurehead was “The Twin Brothers.”

candidates.label: Syrtis Maior (Gulf of Sidra)
candidates.support: A gulf on the northern coast of Africa, off today's Libya, known in ancient geography as Syrtis Maior, whose sandbanks sailors long feared as a hazard; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Roman poet Virgil refers to the danger in the Aeneid. Acts 27:17 says the storm-driven ship's crew, fearing they would run aground there, lowered the sea anchor instead; the ship never reached it. OpenBible.info identifies the Syrtis of Acts 27:17 with the Gulf of Sidra, which Wikidata and Pleiades equate with ancient Syrtis Maior; their points lie about 17 km apart, close for a gulf this size.

scripture.textWEB: After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
